concepts.concept_description: A fundamental approach where organizations identify, assess, and address risks and opportunities that could affect their ability to achieve quality objectives. It requires proactive consideration of what could go wrong and what opportunities exist, rather than reactive problem-solving.
implementation_examples: Using risk registers to document identified risks with severity and probability assessments
Incorporating risk discussions into management review meetings
Applying risk criteria to process design and control measures
Reviewing risks when changes occur to products, processes, or organization
common_misconceptions: Risk-based thinking requires formal risk management systems or software
All risks must be eliminated - misunderstanding that some risks are acceptable with controls
Risk assessment is a one-time activity rather than ongoing
Only negative risks matter - missing opportunities
typical_audit_pitfalls: No evidence of systematic risk identification process
Risks documented but not used to drive decisions or controls
Risk assessments not updated when changes occur
No linkage between identified risks and preventive measures

concepts.concept_description: A discipline that ensures the integrity of products and services throughout their lifecycle by controlling changes to their configuration. It involves identifying configuration items, establishing baselines, controlling changes, and maintaining traceability between requirements, design, production, and support.
implementation_examples: Configuration identification numbering system for all parts and documents
Configuration control boards to review and approve changes
Configuration status accounting records showing current approved configuration
Configuration audits to verify physical configuration matches documentation
Part marking and serialization systems
common_misconceptions: Configuration management only applies to hardware, not software or documentation
Configuration control begins at production - missing design phase
Any engineer can make configuration changes without formal approval
Configuration management is optional for service organizations
typical_audit_pitfalls: Changes made without proper configuration control board review
No clear configuration baselines established
Configuration records not maintained or not current
Parts issued to production don't match approved configuration
Software versions not tracked or controlled

concepts.concept_description: The systematic management of documented information to ensure that only current, approved, and accessible documents are used throughout the organization. It includes approval, review, distribution, revision control, and retention of documents.
implementation_examples: Document control system with approval workflows and revision tracking
Centralized document repository with access controls
Document review schedules to ensure currency
Obsolete document removal from use points
Document templates and standardized formats
common_misconceptions: All documents need formal approval - misunderstanding of 'documented information'
External documents don't need control
Informal work instructions don't need document control
Electronic systems eliminate need for document control procedures
typical_audit_pitfalls: Obsolete documents found in use areas
Documents changed without revision control
No clear approval process or approval signatures missing
External standards not controlled or current versions unknown
Documents not reviewed periodically

concepts.concept_description: Actions taken to eliminate the cause of a nonconformity and prevent recurrence. It goes beyond simply fixing the immediate problem to address root causes through systematic investigation, analysis, and implementation of effective solutions.
implementation_examples: 8D problem-solving methodology for systematic root cause analysis
5 Why analysis to drill down to root causes
Corrective action request (CAR) system with tracking and closure verification
Effectiveness verification after corrective action implementation
Management review of corrective action trends
common_misconceptions: Corrective action is just fixing the immediate problem
All nonconformities require formal corrective action
Corrective action completion means the problem is solved
Corrective action can be closed without effectiveness verification
typical_audit_pitfalls: Root cause analysis not performed or superficial
Corrective actions don't address root causes
No effectiveness verification after implementation
Recurring nonconformities indicate ineffective corrective actions
Corrective action records incomplete or missing

concepts.concept_description: Actions taken to eliminate the cause of potential nonconformities or other potential undesirable situations. It focuses on preventing problems before they occur through proactive identification and mitigation of risks.
implementation_examples: FMEA (Failure Mode and Effects Analysis) to identify potential failures
Risk registers used to trigger preventive actions
Trend analysis of data to identify potential issues before they become problems
Preventive maintenance programs
Supplier risk assessments and mitigation plans
common_misconceptions: Preventive action is the same as risk-based thinking
All risks require preventive actions
Preventive actions must be formal documented processes
Preventive action records must be maintained like corrective actions
typical_audit_pitfalls: No evidence of preventive action activities
Confusion between preventive and corrective actions
Risk identification not leading to preventive measures
Trend analysis not used proactively

concepts.concept_description: A periodic evaluation by top management of the organization's quality management system to ensure its continuing suitability, adequacy, and effectiveness. It involves reviewing performance data, trends, opportunities for improvement, and resource needs.
implementation_examples: Regular management review meetings with agenda and minutes
Review of quality objectives achievement
Analysis of customer feedback and complaints
Review of process performance and product conformity
Decisions on resource allocation and improvement opportunities
common_misconceptions: Management review can be done by quality manager alone
Management review is just a meeting - missing actions and decisions
Review frequency is flexible - not understanding minimum requirements
Review inputs are optional - not mandatory
typical_audit_pitfalls: Management review not attended by top management
Review inputs incomplete or missing
No outputs or decisions from management review
Actions from review not tracked or completed
Review frequency not maintained

concepts.concept_description: A systematic, independent, and documented process for obtaining audit evidence and evaluating it objectively to determine the extent to which audit criteria are fulfilled. It provides confidence in the effectiveness of the quality management system.
implementation_examples: Annual audit program with schedule and scope
Trained internal auditors with demonstrated competence
Audit checklists and procedures
Nonconformity reporting and corrective action tracking
Audit reports and management review of audit results
common_misconceptions: Anyone can perform internal audits without training
Internal auditors can audit their own work
Audits are optional or can be skipped
Nonconformities from internal audits don't require corrective action
typical_audit_pitfalls: Internal auditors not independent of audited areas
Audit program not executed as planned
Audit findings not properly documented
No follow-up on audit findings
Auditor competence not demonstrated

concepts.concept_description: The process of ensuring that external providers (suppliers) meet requirements through evaluation, selection, monitoring, and re-evaluation. It includes approval processes, performance monitoring, and control based on risk.
implementation_examples: Supplier evaluation criteria and approval process
Approved supplier list with status and performance ratings
Supplier audits and assessments
Incoming inspection and verification
Supplier performance monitoring and corrective action processes
common_misconceptions: All suppliers need the same level of control
Supplier approval is a one-time event
Approved supplier list is optional
Self-declaration from suppliers is sufficient
typical_audit_pitfalls: Suppliers used that are not on approved list
Supplier evaluation criteria not applied consistently
No supplier performance monitoring
Suppliers not re-evaluated periodically
Critical suppliers not given appropriate control

concepts.concept_description: The process for identifying, documenting, segregating, and disposing of products or services that do not conform to requirements. It prevents unintended use or delivery of nonconforming products.
implementation_examples: Nonconforming material tags and segregation areas
Nonconformance reporting system
Disposition procedures (scrap, rework, use-as-is, return to supplier)
Authority for disposition decisions
Records of nonconforming product and disposition
common_misconceptions: Nonconforming product can be used without formal disposition
Anyone can make disposition decisions
Segregation is optional for minor nonconformities
Records are not needed if product is scrapped
typical_audit_pitfalls: Nonconforming product not properly identified or segregated
Disposition made by unauthorized personnel
No records of nonconformity or disposition
Use-as-is disposition not properly justified
Nonconformities not triggering corrective action

concepts.concept_description: The set of operations that establish, under specified conditions, the relationship between values indicated by a measuring instrument and corresponding known values of a measurement standard. It ensures measurement equipment provides accurate and reliable results.
implementation_examples: Calibration schedule and recall system
Calibration certificates with traceability to national standards
Calibration status labeling on equipment
Use of equipment outside calibration interval control
Calibration procedures and acceptance criteria
common_misconceptions: Calibration and verification are the same thing
All measurement equipment needs calibration
Calibration certificates don't need review
Equipment can be used beyond calibration due date
typical_audit_pitfalls: Equipment used beyond calibration due date
Calibration certificates not traceable to standards
No calibration schedule or recall system
Calibration status not visible on equipment
Out-of-calibration equipment used on product

concepts.concept_description: The ability to trace the history, application, or location of an item by means of recorded identifications. It enables tracking of products and materials from receipt through production to delivery, and in some cases, through the supply chain.
implementation_examples: Unique identification of products, components, and materials
Lot or batch numbering systems
Traceability records linking materials to finished products
Forward and backward traceability capabilities
Retention of traceability records per requirements
common_misconceptions: Traceability only applies to final products
Traceability records can be destroyed after shipment
Traceability is only needed for recalls
Serial numbers are always required
typical_audit_pitfalls: Traceability records incomplete or missing
Cannot trace finished product back to materials
Traceability requirements not defined
Records not retained for required period
Lost traceability during rework or repair

concepts.concept_description: The ability to apply knowledge and skills to achieve intended results. Organizations must determine necessary competence for personnel performing work affecting quality, and ensure personnel are competent through education, training, or experience.
implementation_examples: Job descriptions defining required competence
Competence matrix showing required vs. demonstrated competence
Training plans and records
Competence evaluation methods
Competence records for all personnel
common_misconceptions: Competence means only formal training
Competence records are optional
Competence is determined once at hiring
Competence requirements don't need to be defined
typical_audit_pitfalls: No defined competence requirements for positions
Competence not evaluated or demonstrated
Training records incomplete or missing
Personnel performing work without required competence
Competence not maintained or updated

concepts.concept_description: Top management's active involvement and demonstration of leadership in establishing, implementing, and maintaining the quality management system. It involves setting direction, establishing quality policy and objectives, and ensuring resources are provided.
implementation_examples: Top management signs quality policy and objectives
Management review meetings attended by top management
Quality objectives established and monitored by leadership
Resources allocated based on quality priorities
Leadership communicates importance of quality to organization
common_misconceptions: Leadership commitment is just signing documents
Quality manager can demonstrate leadership commitment alone
Leadership involvement is optional for small organizations
Commitment is shown once at certification
typical_audit_pitfalls: Top management not attending management review
Quality policy not understood by personnel
Objectives not established by top management
Resources not provided for quality activities
Leadership not visible in quality activities

concepts.concept_description: Measurable goals established at relevant functions, levels, and processes that are consistent with the quality policy. They must be monitored, communicated, and updated as appropriate.
implementation_examples: SMART objectives (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound)
Objectives at organizational and departmental levels
Objectives aligned with quality policy
Regular monitoring and review of objective achievement
Objectives updated based on performance and changes
common_misconceptions: Objectives can be vague or unmeasurable
Objectives set once and never updated
Only top-level objectives needed
Objectives don't need to be communicated
typical_audit_pitfalls: Objectives not measurable or not SMART
Objectives not monitored or reviewed
Objectives not aligned with quality policy
No evidence of objective achievement
Objectives not communicated to relevant personnel

concepts.concept_description: The systematic approach to transitioning individuals, teams, and organizations from a current state to a desired future state. In quality management, it includes planning, evaluating, approving, implementing, and verifying changes to products, processes, or the QMS.
implementation_examples: Change request forms and approval workflows
Impact assessment before change implementation
Change review boards or approval authorities
Verification and validation of changes
Change notification and training of affected personnel
common_misconceptions: All changes require the same level of control
Emergency changes don't need formal control
Change management only applies to products
Changes can be made without impact assessment
typical_audit_pitfalls: Changes made without formal approval
No impact assessment performed
Changes not verified or validated
Affected personnel not notified of changes
Change records incomplete or missing

concepts.concept_description: The systematic process of planning, executing, and verifying the design and development of products to ensure they meet specified requirements. It includes design planning, inputs, outputs, review, verification, validation, and transfer.
implementation_examples: Design and development planning with stages and reviews
Design inputs including requirements and regulatory needs
Design outputs including specifications and drawings
Design reviews at planned stages
Design verification to confirm outputs meet inputs
Design validation to confirm product meets user needs
Design transfer to production processes
common_misconceptions: Design control only applies to new products
Design changes don't need design control
Verification and validation are the same
Design control is optional for service organizations
typical_audit_pitfalls: Design activities not planned
Design inputs not defined or incomplete
Design reviews not conducted or not documented
Design verification not performed
Design validation missing or incomplete
Design transfer not planned or executed

concepts.concept_description: A comprehensive inspection performed on the first production part or batch to verify that manufacturing processes are capable of producing products that meet all specified requirements. It provides evidence that the production process is ready.
implementation_examples: FAI performed on first production part or batch
All characteristics measured and documented
FAI report includes all drawings, specifications, and results
FAI approved before full production release
FAI repeated when changes affect product characteristics
common_misconceptions: FAI is only needed once per product
FAI can be skipped for simple products
FAI is the same as regular inspection
FAI approval is not required
typical_audit_pitfalls: FAI not performed before production
FAI incomplete - not all characteristics inspected
FAI reports incomplete or missing
FAI not repeated after process changes
FAI approval authority unclear

concepts.concept_description: A comprehensive program to detect, avoid, prevent, and mitigate the risk of counterfeit or suspect unapproved parts entering the supply chain. It includes supplier controls, part verification, and reporting mechanisms.
implementation_examples: Counterfeit parts prevention policy and procedures
Supplier approval with focus on authorized sources
Part verification and authentication processes
Suspicious parts reporting and quarantine procedures
Training on counterfeit part detection
Records of parts received and sources
common_misconceptions: Counterfeit prevention is only for expensive parts
Authorized distributors always prevent counterfeits
Visual inspection is sufficient
Counterfeit prevention is optional
typical_audit_pitfalls: No counterfeit prevention program
Suppliers not verified as authorized sources
Parts received without verification
No suspicious parts reporting process
Personnel not trained on counterfeit detection

concepts.concept_description: Foreign Object Debris/Damage (FOD) prevention programs designed to prevent introduction of foreign objects into products that could cause damage or failure. Critical in aerospace manufacturing and maintenance.
implementation_examples: FOD prevention procedures and training
Clean work areas and FOD awareness zones
Tool accountability and control systems
Personal item restrictions in work areas
FOD walk-downs and inspections
FOD reporting and corrective action
common_misconceptions: FOD is only relevant in final assembly
Small objects can't cause significant damage
FOD prevention is just cleaning
FOD prevention doesn't apply to service organizations
typical_audit_pitfalls: No FOD prevention program
Work areas not controlled for FOD
Tools not accounted for
Personnel not trained on FOD prevention
FOD incidents not investigated

concepts.concept_description: Processes where the resulting output cannot be verified by subsequent monitoring or measurement, so deficiencies become apparent only after the product is in use or the service has been delivered. These require validation.
implementation_examples: Identification of special processes (welding, heat treatment, coating, etc.)
Process validation including equipment, personnel, and parameters
Process qualification and certification
Ongoing monitoring of process parameters
Personnel qualification for special processes
Revalidation when changes occur
common_misconceptions: All manufacturing processes are special processes
Special process validation is one-time
Process monitoring is not needed after validation
Personnel training is sufficient without validation
typical_audit_pitfalls: Special processes not identified
Special processes not validated
Process parameters not monitored
Personnel not qualified
Validation not repeated after changes

concepts.concept_description: Confirmation through objective evidence that processes consistently produce results meeting predetermined requirements. For special processes, validation is mandatory before use.
implementation_examples: Installation Qualification (IQ) - equipment properly installed
Operational Qualification (OQ) - process operates as designed
Performance Qualification (PQ) - process produces acceptable product
Process validation protocols and reports
Statistical analysis of process capability
Revalidation triggers and schedules
common_misconceptions: Validation and verification are the same
One successful run is sufficient validation
Validation is permanent
Process parameters can be changed without revalidation
typical_audit_pitfalls: Processes requiring validation not identified
Validation protocols incomplete
Statistical evidence not provided
Validation not documented
Revalidation not performed after changes
